  • Attachment to mucosal surfacesp. 10

  • Acute Gastroenteritis (Diarrheal Diseases)p. 2

  • Watery (Non-Bloody) Diarrheap. 3

CELLULAR STRUCTURE5
  • LPS acts as a barrier to toxic molecules (like certain antibiotics) and functions as an endotoxin (O-antigen) that triggers strong immune response in humansp. 1
  • Contains a thin layer of peptidoglycan (which provides structural integrity and shape) and enzymes involved in nutrient transport and antibiotic degradationp. 1
  • For examplep. 1
    • Type 1 Pili allows E. coli to bind to bladder cells causing UTIs, while sex pili enable the transfer of genetic material (like antibiotic resistant plasmids) to other bacteria via conjugation
  • These replicate independently of the main chromosome and often carry non-essential but highly advantageous genes, such as those encoding antibiotic resistance or toxins.p. 1
  • Scattered throughout the cytoplasm, these molecular machines translate genetic code into proteins and are the targets for several classes of antibiotics.p. 1
MANAGEMENT: THERAPEUTIC INTERVENTIONS ESCHERICHIA2
  • Antibiotic restrictions in EHEC / STEC with Shiga-toxin producing E. coli to prevent antibiotic-induced stress triggering acute kidney failure ( HUS )p. 3
  • Complicated UTIs / Pyelonephritisp. 3
    • Ceftriaxone or Ciprofloxacin
Treatment1
  • Antimicrobial stewardship & hospital infection controlp. 3

PATHOGENESIS OF SALMONELLA2
  • Invasion - Salmonella invades M cells (microfold cells), specialized immune-monitoring cells found in Peyer's patches of ileump. 4
  • vs lysosomal digestion Inside Salmonella-Containing Vacuole (SCV), Salmonella activates SPI-2 (TIII-2) which encodes for proteins that modify SCV preventing lysosomes from digesting it enabling Salmonella to continue multiplying.p. 4
HOST RESPONSE OF SALMONELLA5
  • Innate Immune Activation (Pyroptosis)p. 4
  • TLR4 detects O-antigen/ LPS cell wall & TLR5 detects H-antigen/ flagella proteinp. 4

MICROSCOPIC MORPHOLOGY1

  • Stool and urine cultures (second and third weeks)p. 5
  • The agar is cracked or pushed up (gas production)p. 5
  • Vi Antigen Maskp. 5
    • boil bacterial suspension for 15 minutes to melt away the heat-labile Vi capsule , then repeat the O-antigen test.
  • Serological Tests (The Widal Test)p. 5
  • Multiplex PCR Panels & MALDI-TOF Mass Spectrometryp. 5
CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS OF SALMONELLA INFECTIONS1

MANAGEMENT: THERAPEUTIC INTERVENTIONS6
  • NO treatment for healthy individuals with standard food poisoning (usually self-limiting)p. 5
  • Avoid antibiotics that alter gut flora in uncomplicated casesp. 5
  • Ciprofloxacin or Ceftriaxone for bacteremia of high-risk groups (infants < 3 months , adults >65, and immunocompromised individualsp. 5
  • Empiric First-Line Therapyp. 5
    • Ceftriaxone (IV for hospitalized cases) or oral fluoroquinolones like Ciprofloxacin ; Managing Multi-Drug Resistance (MDR): oral Azithromycin
  • Personal and Food Hygienep. 5
  • Vaccination against Salmonella Typhi, particularly for travelers, healthcare workers, and communities with vulnerable sanitation infrastructurep. 5

PATHOGENESIS OF SHIGELLA4
  • Multi-step mucosal barrier invasionp. 6
  • Lateral invasionp. 6
  • Shigella produces IcsA (VirG) Protein to hijack actin which polymerizes behind bacterium, forming a "rocket tail” which propels Shigella to spread horizontally through the tissue, completely avoiding the outside immune system 2.

  • It is one of the leading causes of global diarrheal mortality, particularly among children under five in low- and middle-income nations.p. 5
SHIGELLA IN THE PHILIPPINES3
  • Locally under "Acute Bloody Diarrhea" within the Philippine Integrated DiseaseSurveillance and Response (PIDSR) systemp. 6

CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS OF SHIGELLA INFECTIONS4
  • Shigella sonnei causing mild, watery diarrheap. 6

  • Shigella is highly infectiousp. 6
  • Allowing as few as 10 to 100 bacterial cells is enough to cause severe illness (bacillary/dysentery).This low infectious dose is due to Shigella's unique ability to survive harsh, highly acidic environments of the human stomachp. 6
DIAGNOSIS: DIAGNOSTIC LABORATORIES7

  • Salmonella-Shigella (SS) Agarp. 6
  • Xylose Lysine Deoxycholate (XLD) Agarp. 6
  • Serogrouping and Agglutination Testingp. 6
GRAM NEGATIVE, ENTERIC RODS (BACILLI) | LECTURER’S NAME1
  • Test culture or stool sample using an ELISA kit or PCR to directly detect the presence of Shiga toxins (Stx)p. 7
MANAGEMENT: THERAPEUTIC INTERVENTIONS4
  • Fluid and Electrolyte Resuscitationp. 7
  • Targeted Antimicrobial Therapyp. 7
  • First-Line Choicesp. 7
    • azithromycin or ciprofloxacin , intravenous ceftriaxone
  • Strict anti-diarrheal contraindicationp. 7
PREVENTION: HEALTH PROMOTION & DISEASE PREVENTION4
  • Rigorous Personal and Contact Hygienep. 7
  • Handwash; isolation precautions; disinfectionp. 7
  • Food and Water Safety (WASH Initiatives)p. 7

ANTIGENIC STRUCTURES1
  • Made of the protein flagellin, these spiral filaments are anchored directly into the cell envelope.p. 9
STRUCTURAL CHARACTERISTICS1
  • The outer lipid A portion acts as an endotoxin , triggering severe inflammation and sepsis if it enters the bloodstream.p. 8
    • The variable O-antigen chain is used to classify the bacteria into specific serotypes
PATHOGENESIS OF PROTEUS7
  • Swarming Motility and Adherencep. 9
  • Upon touching solid surface (like bladder wall or catheter), Proteus transforms into elongated, hyper-flagellated "swarm cells" packed with thousands of H (flagellar) antigensp. 9
  • Allows rapid gliding across surfaces in wave-like motions (allowing Proteus to travel up urethra against flow of urine)p. 9
  • Once the bacteria reach their destination, it switches back to short cells and deploy MR/P fimbriae (Mannose- Resistant Proteus-like pili ) to lock tightly onto the surface cells of bladder or kidneysp. 9
  • Proteus produces urease in massive quantities, which hydrolyzes urea into ammonia (NH3) and carbamate.p. 9
  • Crystal Precipitation and Stone Formationp. 9
  • Proteus traps mineral crystals within a sticky matrix of sugars and proteins to form dense biofilm on the surfaces of urinary catheters.p. 9
CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS OF PROTEUS INFECTIONS4
  • Complicated Urinary Tract Infections (UTIs)p. 9
  • Cystitis, dysuria, urgency and frequency, suprapubic pain, strong ammonia odor, pyuria and hematuriap. 9
  • Urinary Stones (Struvite / Staghorn Calculi)p. 9
  • Alkaline environment created by bacteria causes magnesium and phosphate minerals to crystallize directly over the bacterial colonies (stone formation), renal colic, staghorn calculi, persistent infectionp. 9
COMPLICATIONS AND EMERGENCIES OF PROTEUS4
  • High fever & chills, costovertebral Angle (CVA) Tenderness, nausea and vomitingp. 10
  • Catheter-Associated UTIs (CAUTI)p. 10
  • In hospitals or long-term care facilities, Proteus forms a thick, crystalline crust inside urinary drainage tubes resulting in catheter blockage, autonomic dysreflexiap. 10
  • Wound Infections such as diabetic foot ulcers, pressure sores (bedsores), and burn wounds, bacteremia and septic shockp. 10
DIAGNOSTIC LABORATORIES7
  • Specimen Collection and Direct Microscopyp. 10
    • Blood culture bottles (for sepsis )p. 10
    • Under a light microscope, Gram-negative , straight, rod-shaped bacilli.p. 10
    • Blood Agar and Nutrient Agarp. 10
    • Rapid Screening Bench Testsp. 10
  • Oxidase Testp. 10
    • Negative . Catalase Test: Positive
  • Phenylalanine Deaminase (PAD) Testp. 10
    • Positive . slant with distinct deep hunter green
  • Diagnostic Serologyp. 10
    • The Weil-Felix Test
PATHOGENESIS OF PROTEUS1
  • Crystalline biofilm seals bacteria inside, completely blocking out antibiotics and preventing immune system from reaching themp. 9
MANAGEMENT: THERAPEUTIC INTERVENTIONS3
  • Targeted Antimicrobial Therapyp. 10
  • First-line oral choicesp. 10
    • Ampicillin, Cephalexin, Ciprofloxacin
  • Acetohydroxamic Acid (AHA) for patients with chronic, un-resectable Proteus stonesp. 10
PREVENTION: HEALTH PROMOTION AND DISEASE PREVENTION4
  • Catheter care to prevent a Proteus catheter-associated UTI (CAUTI); Continuous closed drainage to prevent contaminated urine from flowing backward into the bodyp. 10
  • Dietary and Urine Acidificationp. 10
  • Hydration; ascorbic acid; proanthocyanidinp. 10
  • Hospital Contact Precautionsp. 10

Foundational lecture framework p. 1
(AEROBIC & ANAEROBIC)
(AEROBIC & ANAEROBIC)13
  • PROCESS OF SPORULATION AND GERMINATIONp. 1
  • Two Formsp. 1
  • Vegetative Cellp. 1
  • Develop under favorable conditions such as: (+) nutrients, (+) temperature, (+) moisturep. 1
  • Endosporesp. 1
  • Sporulation occurs under unfavorable conditions (e.g., low moisture and nutrients)p. 1
  • Become dormant and resistantp. 1
  • Spore Resistance Extremely resistant to chemical & physical environments. Viable for years in contaminated pasteur Inactivated at 120 oC for 15 mins (autoclave)p. 1
  • Contain all genetic materials, enclosed in several protein coats & are resistant to heat, drying & most chemicalsp. 1
  • Eventually, spores germinate back into their vegetative form in moist & nutrient-rich surfaces at the right temperature (37 oC) of sporeformer bacillip. 1
  • They are in spore form if they are in soil/dead animals (depleted nutrients).p. 1
  • The spores of the bacillus are short-chain, flat-ended, vegetative cells.p. 1
  • In living animals and humans, they are not sporulated (vegetative form).p. 1

  • For animalsp. 2
    • Active immunization of live spore vaccine (Stearne strain)
  • For manp. 2
    • Killed spore vaccine to control outbreak Terrorists used Bacillus anthracis as a biological weapon. Letters containing anthrax spores were mailed to several news media and 2 senators. Killing 5 persons and 17 were infected

Anaerobes

13 rows
Foundational lecture framework pp. 1–3
GENERAL
General10
  • ANAEROBESp. 1
  • Bacterial action against toxic products of oxygen, such as:p. 1
  • O2-: superoxide anionp. 1
  • H2O2: hydrogen peroxidep. 1
  • OH: hydroxyl radical Aerobic & Facultative Aerobes Anaerobesp. 1
  • Cytochrome systems for the metabolisms of O2p. 1
  • Cytochrome function as electron transfer agent in many metabolic pathways especially in the cellular respirationp. 1
  • Catalase catalyzes the reduction of H2O2 into water and oxygenp. 1
  • Superoxide dismutase (SOD) catalyzes Superoxide radical (O- into ordinary molecular O2p. 1
  • DON’T have Cytochrome systemsp. 1
(O2)
(O2)2
  • May or may not have catalase.p. 1
  • Low levels of SODp. 1
OBLIGATE ANAEROBES
OBLIGATE ANAEROBES2
  • Usually lack SOD and catalasep. 1
  • Susceptible to the lethal effects of Oxygenp. 1
ENVIRONMENTS WHERE ANAEROBES SURVIVE
ENVIRONMENTS WHERE ANAEROBES SURVIVE18
  • The area or environment with very low REDOX potential allow anaerobes to survive, which may be found in:p. 1
  • Oropharynxp. 1
  • Colonp. 1
  • Deep skin appendages (where mucosal surfaces and oxygen is low)p. 1
  • Devitalized tissuesp. 1
  • Ischemic tissuesp. 1
  • Abscessp. 1
  • OXYGEN REQUIREMENTS OF ORGANISMSp. 1
  • Oxygen is very toxic to anaerobic organisms, and the amount of oxygen decreases toward the bottom of the test tube.p. 1
  • Obligate aerobe grows where there is 20-21% O2.p. 1
  • Microaerophiles will grow where there is about 5% O2.p. 1
  • Obligate anaerobes grow in 0% O2.p. 1
  • Examples:p. 1
  • Mycobacterium tuberculosis is an obligate aerobe, which is why it prefers to reside in the lungs.p. 1
  • Obligate anaerobes include Clostridium tetani, Bacteroides, Fusobacterium, and Peptostreptococcus.p. 1
  • Facultative anaerobes can grow in very small amounts of oxygen, such as enterics and other Staphylococcus.p. 1
  • Aerotolerant anaerobes include Campylobacter jejuni, an enteric.p. 1
  • Helicobacter pylori is a microaerophile, a curved gram negative rod that can cause peptic ulcer syndrome. Infectionsp. 1
ANAEROBIC INFECTION
ANAEROBIC INFECTION28
  • All anaerobic infections are polymicrobial, which means that there is more than one organism in that infection.p. 1
  • For example, E. coli or other facultative anaerobes are present with obligate anaerobes, the facultative anaerobes will consume the oxygen. This makes the environment more anaerobic and will allow the multiplication of anaerobes, leading to infection.p. 1
  • SOURCES OF ANAEROBES Exogenous Endogenousp. 2
  • Gained entrance through trauma or ingestionp. 2
  • Example:p. 2
  • Clostridium tetani Clostridium botulinum Fusobacterium necrophorump. 2
  • Normal flora Microbiota Anaerobes Skinp. 2
  • Cutibacterium acnes ( 💬 previously Propionibacterium acnes; causes acne)p. 2
  • Peptostreptococcus Female Genital Tractp. 2
  • Gm (-) Bacilli Porphyromonas Prevotella bivia/disiensp. 2
  • Gm (+) Bacilli Lactobacilli Clostridium Oral Cavityp. 2
  • Gm (-) Bacilli Porphyromonas Prevotella bivia/disiens Fusobacterium nucleatump. 2
  • 💬 Note its difference with F. necrophorum, which is not a normal florap. 2
  • Gm (+) Filamentous Actinomycesp. 2
  • Ratio of 100 Anaerobes : 1 Aerobe Colonp. 2
  • Gm (-) Bacilli Bacteroides grp (fragilis) Prevotella bivia/disiens Fusobacterium nucleatump. 2
  • Gm (+) Bacilli Clostridium (C. perfringens, C. difficile) Bifidobacterium Eubacteriump. 2
  • Ratio 1000 Anaerobes: 1 Aerobep. 2
  • Characteristics of Obligate Anaerobic Infectionsp. 2
  • Almost all anaerobic infections originate from the patient’s own microflora, which means that endogenous anaerobes are opportunistic pathogens.p. 2
  • 💬 If the normal flora leave their normal habitat, they become pathogenic.p. 2
  • Predisposing factors to endogenous anaerobic infections:p. 2
  • 💬 Vascular disease - less blood or oxygenp. 2
  • Traumap. 2
  • 💬 Surgery - accidentally puncturing an area causes anaerobes to travel to another area.p. 2
  • Presence of foreign bodiesp. 2
  • Malignancyp. 2
  • This could result in poor blood supply, tissue necrosis, and low oxidation-reduction potential, favoring the growth of anaerobic bacteria.p. 2
CLUES TO DIAGNOSIS FOR ANAEROBIC INFECTIONS
CLUES TO DIAGNOSIS FOR ANAEROBIC INFECTIONS7
  • Infections adjacent to a mucosal surfacep. 2
  • 💬 The colon and oral cavity are mucosal areas that contain a lot of mixed organisms.p. 2
  • Foul-smelling lesion or dischargep. 2
  • 💬 Due to the short-chain fatty acid metabolism of anaerobic infections.p. 2
  • Necrotic gangrenous tissue (gas gangrene)p. 2
  • 💬 There is increased CO2 or H2 in the tissue.p. 2
  • Bacteremia or endocarditis with NO growth on aerobic blood culturep. 2
OTHER CLUES TO DIAGNOSIS FOR ANAEROBIC INFECTIONS
OTHER CLUES TO DIAGNOSIS FOR ANAEROBIC INFECTIONS12
  • Infection following a human or animal bitep. 2
  • 💬 Oral cavity contains lots of mixed flora with anaerobic organisms that cause infectionp. 2
  • e.g., clenched-fist injuryp. 2
  • Abscess formationp. 2
  • Infection related to the use of antibiotics effective against aerobes onlyp. 2
  • 💬 Antibiotics will kill aerobes only to allow anaerobes to overgrow.p. 2
  • e.g., aminoglycosidesp. 2
  • Black discoloration exudates containing pigmented Prevotellap. 2
  • or Porphyromonas spp.p. 2
  • “Sulfur granules” in discharge caused by Actinomycetesp. 2
  • 💬 Other bacteria and fungi can also produce sulfur granules like Mycetoma.p. 2
  • LABORATORY DIAGNOSIS FOR ANAEROBIC INFECTIONSp. 2
01 | COLLECTION OF SPECIMENS
01 | COLLECTION OF SPECIMENS8
  • All specimens should be collected aseptically.p. 2
  • Acceptable specimensp. 2
  • Blood specimenp. 2
  • Abscess contentsp. 2
  • Deep aspirates of woundsp. 2
  • Urine collected by percutaneous suprapubic bladder aspirationp. 2
  • Needle aspirates of an abscessp. 2
  • Aspirates of body fluids (pleural, pericardial, cerebrospinal, peritoneal, and joint fluids)p. 2
02 | TRANSPORT OF SPECIMENS
02 | TRANSPORT OF SPECIMENS9
  • Anaerobic disposable plastic bag (Resazurin Indicators)p. 2
  • 💬 Place in bag/transport materials with minimal oxygen and label if it is aerobic or anaerobicp. 2
  • 💬 Contains indicators whether oxygen has been removed successfullyp. 2
  • 💬 Bag is heat-sealedp. 2
  • Fluid transport (anaerobic/aerobic)p. 2
  • Anaerobic transport kitp. 2
  • Prompt delivery of specimens to the lab is essential.p. 2
  • 💬 If an anaerobic specimen is to be processed, inform the laboratory ahead of time that they may prepare the needed materials.p. 2
  • 💬 After collecting the specimen, you have to work in an anaerobic glove-box with less oxygen (with at least 20% CO2).p. 2
03 | CULTURE AND IDENTIFICATION
03 | CULTURE AND IDENTIFICATION11
  • Anaerobes are hard to isolate and are often not recovered from infected sites.p. 2
  • Isolate specimens in plates (e.g., blood-agar plate with vitamin K & hemin, sheep’s blood)p. 2

Spirochetes and Atypical Bacteria

13 rows
Foundational lecture framework p. 1
GENERAL
General19
  • KEY CHARACTERISTICSp. 1
  • Long, slender, helically coiled, spiral or corkscrew-shaped bacilli.p. 1
  • Gram-negativep. 1
  • Motilep. 1
  • One family of the order Spirochaetales consists of two genera whose members are human pathogens: Borrelia and Treponema. 📖p. 1
  • The other family includes one genus of medical importance: Leptospira.📖p. 1
  • The spirochetes have many structural characteristics in common as typified by Treponema pallidum.p. 1
  • STRUCTURAL CHARACTERISTICSp. 1
  • Outer sheath (glycosaminoglycan coating)p. 1
  • Outer membrane (found inside the sheath)p. 1
  • Contains peptidoglycan 📖p. 1
  • Maintains the structural integrity of the organisms.p. 1
  • Endoflagella (axial filaments)p. 1
  • Flagella-like organelles in the periplasmic space encased by the outer membrane.p. 1
  • Begin at each end of the organism and they wind around it, extending to and overlapping at the midpoint.p. 1
  • Inner membrane (cytoplasmic membrane)p. 1
  • Inside the endoflagellap. 1
  • Provides osmotic stability and it covers the protoplasmic cylinder.p. 1
  • A series of cytoplasmic tubules or body fibrils are inside the cell near the inner membrane.p. 1

Treponema pallidum
Syphilis
pp. 1–3
General1
  • Treponema pallidum is the causative agent of the sexually transmitted infection called syphilis .p. 1
02 | ANTIGENIC STRUCTURES OF T. PALLIDUM6
  • The outer membrane surrounds the periplasmic space and the peptidoglycan cytoplasmic membrane complex.p. 1
  • Membrane proteins are present that contain covalently bound lipids at their amino terminals.p. 1
  • Lipids appear to anchor the proteins to the cytoplasmic or the outer membranes and keep the proteins inaccessible to antibodies.p. 1
  • The endoflagella are in the periplasmic space. 📖p. 2
  • Has a hyaluronidase that breaks down the hyaluronic acid in the ground substance of tissue and presumably enhances the invasiveness of the organism.p. 2
  • Cardiolipin is an important component of the treponemal antigens.p. 2
(MHA-TP)1
  • More prone to non-specific agglutination.p. 3
03 | PATHOGENESIS OF ACQUIRED AND CONGENITAL SYPHILIS7
  • Transmission is primarily through sexual contact.p. 2
  • Spirochetes multiply locally at the site of entry.p. 2
  • Granulomatous lesions (gummas) in the skin, bones, and liver.p. 2
  • aortitis, aortic aneurysm, aortic valve insufficiency.p. 2
  • Treponemes are very rare in tertiary lesions.p. 2
  • PATHOGENESIS OF CONGENITAL SYPHILISp. 2
  • childhood, which include:p. 2
    • In congenital infection, the child makes IgM anti-treponemal antibodies.p. 2
03 | PATHOGENESIS OF ACQUIRED AND CONGENITAL SYPHILIS7
  • PATHOGENESIS OF ACQUIRED SYPHILIS Stage of Disease Signs and Symptoms Pathogenesis Initial Contact (2–10 wks., depends on inoculum size)p. 2
  • May also present with syphilitic meningitis , chorioretinitis, hepatitis, nephritis, or periostitis.p. 2
  • Multiplication and dissemination of spirochetes produce lesions in the skin and mucous membranes.p. 2
    • Stage of Disease Signs and Symptoms Pathogenesis recur within 3–5 years after infection; thereafter the individual is not infectious.
  • Infection may remain subclinical — the patient may pass through the primary or secondary stage (or both) without symptoms and still develop tertiary lesions.p. 2
    • Latent Syphilis
  • No clinical signs or symptoms.p. 2
  • Occurs in the remainder of untreated cases (disease progresses to the tertiary stage).p. 2
  • Others are born alive but they develop the signs of congenital syphilis inp. 2
Laboratory Diagnosis8
  • CSFp. 2
    • Venereal Disease Research Lab ( VDRL ) testing
  • SEROLOGIC TEST FOR SYPHILISp. 3
    • NON-TREPONEMAL TEST
  • Rapid Plasma Reagin ( RPR ), Venereal Disease Research Laboratory ( VDRL ) Test, Toluidine Red Unheated Serum Test (TRUST)p. 3
  • Positive non-treponemal tests develop after 2–3 weeks of untreated syphilis , and they are positive in high titer in secondary syphilis .p. 3
  • SEROLOGIC TEST FOR SYPHILISp. 3
    • TREPONEMAL TEST
  • The treponemal tests measure antibodies against Treponema pallidum antigens.p. 3
  • These tests are used to determine if a positive result from a non-treponemal test is truly positive or falsely positive .p. 3
  • The traditional treponemal tests are less useful as screening tests because once positive after initial syphilitic infection, the tests remain positive for life independent of therapy for syphilis .p. 3
03 | PATHOGENESIS OF ACQUIRED AND CONGENITAL SYPHILIS1
  • Adequate treatment of the mother during pregnancy prevents congenital syphilis .p. 2
05 | TREATMENT OF SYPHILIS3
  • Penicillinp. 3
    • treatment of choice
  • Older or latent syphilisp. 3
    • Benzathine penicillin G IM once weekly for 3 weeks .
  • Neurosyphilisp. 3
    • IV penicillin G
06 | PREVENTION AND CONTROL OF SYPHILIS4
  • Prompt and adequate treatment of all discovered cases.p. 3
  • Follow-up on sources of infection and contacts so they can be treated.p. 3
  • Abstinence, monogamous relationships, and effective and correct use of condoms.p. 3
  • Congenital syphilis before the 4th month of pregnancy.p. 3

General6

  • Main Reservoirp. 4

Borrelia burgdorferi
Lyme disease
pp. 4–5
General4
  • Easily isolated from erythema migrans skin lesions.p. 4
  • Spiral, 20–30um long and 0.2–0.3 widep. 4
  • Have variable numbers (7–11) of endoflagella and are highly motilep. 4

    • Barbour-Stoenner-Kelly medium
03 | EPIDEMIOLOGY4
  • Reservoirsp. 5
    • Mice, deer, other rodents, and birds.
  • Vector for transmissionp. 5
    • Ixodes tick
  • Transmission occurs through saliva infection during feeding.p. 5
  • Longer attachment is associated with higher risk of transmission ( 36–72 hours ).p. 5
 —
General1
  • Borrelia Burgdorferi is another species under the genus Borrelia and it is the causative agent of Lyme Disease .p. 4
01 | PATHOGENESIS AND CLINICAL FINDINGS7
  • 3–4 weeks after the tick bite.p. 4
  • Flat reddened area near the tick bite and slowly expands with central clearingp. 4
  • Fever, Chills, Myalgia, Headachep. 4
  • Arthralgia, arthritis, neurologic manifestations with meningitis , facial nerve palsy, painful radiculopathy; Cardiac disease with conduction defects and myopericarditisp. 4
  • Chronic skin, nervous system, or joint involvement.p. 4
  • Transmission of the Borrelia burgdorferi to humans is by injection of the organism in tick saliva, or by regurgitation of the ticks’ midgut contents.p. 4
  • Lyme disease , similar to other spirochetal diseases, occurs in stages with early and late manifestations.p. 5
02 | DIAGNOSTIC LABORATORY TESTS8
  • Serology has been the main test for the diagnosis of Lyme disease .p. 5
  • Serology for Lyme disease should only be done when there are highly suggestive clinical findings.p. 5
  • Serologic testing is neither required nor recommended.p. 5
  • If the cause of the skin lesion is in doubt and empiric antimicrobial therapy is not administered, serologic testing is reasonable.p. 5
  • In patients with non-EM presentations, you can perform the 2-tiered serologic testing.p. 5
  • The traditional 2-tiered serologic testing algorithm starts with a sensitive enzyme immunoassay (EIA) or immunofluorescence assay (IFA).p. 5
  • Positive resultsp. 5
    • would need more specific serologic test, IgM and IgG Western blot.
  • Another way to diagnose early Lyme disease is by performing preliminary polymerase chain reaction ( PCR ) testing for Borrelia burgdorferi on a skin punch biopsy of at least 2mm diameter taken from the margin of the skin lesion.p. 5
05 | TREATMENT, PREVENTION, AND CONTROL8
  • Treatment of the following for 14–21 days:p. 5
  • Doxycyclinep. 5
    • more effective than amoxicillin for late manifestations
  • Cefuroximep. 5
  • Ceftriaxonep. 5
    • effective mostly for refractory cases
  • Avoidance of exposure to ticksp. 5
  • Wearing of long sleeves and long pants tucked into socksp. 5
  • Careful examination of skin for ticks after being outdoorsp. 5
  • Application of insecticidesp. 5
Leptospira
LeptospirosisWeil’s disease
pp. 5–7
02 | TRANSMISSION7
  • Infected animals (mammals) shed Leptospira via urine:p. 5
    • Rodents (most important reservoir) excrete leptospirae in urine both during the active illness and during the asymptomatic carrier state.p. 5
      • Household pets (i.e. dogs) Domesticated livestock (i.e. swine, cattle)
    • Leptospires are spread by the urine of infected animals (rodents, dogs, livestock, pigs, horses, and wildlife)p. 5
  • Humans can be infected through:p. 5
    • Direct contact with the urine or reproductive fluids from infected animals.p. 5
      • Contact with urine-contaminated water (floodwater, rivers, streams, sewage) and wet soil.
      • Ingestion
    • or urine-contaminated waterp. 5
  • Notep. 5
    • Leptospirae remains viable in stagnant water for several weeks. So, drinking, swimming, bathing or food contamination may lead to human infection.
  • Transmission occurs through mucous membranes, conjunctiva, and skin cuts or abrasions.p. 5
03 | PATHOGENESIS8

  • Adherence factors such as outer membrane proteinsp. 5
    • binds the host extracellular matrix (ECM).
  • Enzymesp. 5
    • hydrolyze ECM and some activate the complement system. Incubation Period ( 2-30 days )
  • Toxins released lead to breakdown of vessel walls and fluid leakage.p. 6
  • IgM and IgG antibodies directed against Leptospira are generated by the host.p. 6

03 | PATHOGENESIS2

    • performed on first 10 days
  • CSFp. 6
    • first week of illness
  • Polymerase Chain Reaction ( PCR ) has the advantage of early confirmation of the diagnosis especially during the acute leptospiremic phase (first week of illness) before the appearance of antibodies.p. 6
  • INDIRECT DETECTION METHODp. 6
    • Serologic methods are becoming more widely used, becoming effective after the 6th day after onset of symptoms.p. 6
    • Specific IgM Rapid Diagnostic Tests like LeptoDipstick®, Leptospira IgM ELISA (PanBio), MCAT and Dridot®, are serologic tests in a single test format for the quick detection of Leptospira genus-specific lgM antibodies in human sera.p. 6

  • Doxycycline is the drug of choice.p. 6

08 | PREVENTION AND CONTROL4
  • Wear protective boots and gloves during the rainy season.p. 7

Walking pneumonia

General6
  • Facultative anaerobep. 8

  • It attaches to the respiratory epithelium using a specialized attachment organelle containing adhesion protein P1 at its tip.p. 8

  • After attachment, the bacteria release:p. 8
    • In the alveoli, bacteria may be phagocytosed by alveolar macrophages.p. 8
  • This activates an inflammatory cascade involving:p. 8
    • Lymphocytes Impaired mucociliary clearancep. 8
    • Decreased ciliary function leads to reduced clearance of mucus and pathogens.p. 8
    • This promotes further bacterial spread into the lungs and progression of infection.p. 8

  • Therefore, a negative cold agglutinin test does not rule out infection.p. 9

Rickettsia spp.
R. rickettsiiR. prowazekiiR. typhiR. akariScrub typhus
pp. 12–14
01 | IMPORTANT PROPERTIES8
  • The Rickettsia are pleomorphic, non-mobile, coccobacilli.p. 12
  • Classically considered gram-negative bacteria.p. 12
  • These organisms are obligate, intracellular pathogensp. 12
  • They can survive only inside cells, and this is because they can’t make 2 important energetic compounds by themselves (Coenzyme A and NAD+).p. 12
    • Instead, they need to get them from other eukaryotic cells.
  • They are transmitted from some animal or other vector source which is outside of the human being.p. 12
    • Rickettsia rickettsii: from tick bites Rickettsia prowazekii: from lice feces Ricketisia typhi: from rat fleas
  • As seen in Figure 44, several arthropods may serve as vectors.p. 12
  • They are most commonly the ticks, the mites, and the fleas.p. 12
  • It also shows the corresponding mammalian reservoirs.p. 12
Virulence Factors6
  • Rickettsiae to Endothelial Cellsp. 12
  • The Rickettsias start by adhering to the endothelial cell with the help of OmpA and OmpB surface protein.p. 12
  • Within that cell they have a slow replicative process.p. 12
  • Spreadp. 12
  • Eventually they are able to spread as they shed from the infected cells having released themselves through cell lysis.p. 12
  • It is through cell lysis which finally exposes the Rickettsia to the human immune system and its recognition is able to start the systemic response.p. 12
01 | IMPORTANT PROPERTIES1
  • The incidence of disease depends on the geographic distribution of arthropod vectors and on the risk of exposure, which is enhanced by conditions such as poor hygiene and camping.p. 12
03 | CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS AND EPIDEMIOLOGY7
  • Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever is caused by Rickettsia rickettsii.p. 13
  • The disease is characterized by non-specific symptoms such as fever, myalgia, and headache.p. 13
  • After 3–5 days of illness, the typical rash (macular rash) turns into petechiae.p. 13
  • The rash in Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever begins in the extremities, and then moves centripetally, and it involves the palms and soles.p. 13
  • Fever, headache, malaise, myalgias, arthralgias and nausea.p. 13
  • Mild disease with vesicular rash resembling varicella.p. 13
  • Rash is characterized by an eschar which is a punched out ulcer covered with blackened scab.p. 13
04 | LABORATORY DIAGNOSIS2
  • Laboratory diagnosis of rickettsial diseases is based on serologic tests rather than isolation of the organism from cultures.p. 14
  • Rickettsia culture can be done, grown in cell culture or embryonated eggs; but it is a hazardous procedure and must be performed in a biosafety level 3 laboratory.p. 14
SEROLOGIC TESTS6
  • Serologic tests are only used to confirm the diagnosis, which primarily, should be based on clinical findings.p. 14
  • Indirect Immunofluorescence Antibody ( ELISA )p. 14
  • Most widely used method because of the availability of the reagents and the ease with which it can be performed.p. 14
  • Can be used to detect rickettsia in thick secretion of tissuesp. 14
  • Also useful in the detection of Rickettsia rickettsii, in skin biopsy specimen of rocky mountain spotted fever, scrub typhus , and other rickettsial diseases.p. 14
  • Allows the diagnosis before a serologic response.p. 14
05 | TREATMENT AND PREVENTION7
  • Tetracyclines (e.g. doxycycline ) are the primary drugs of choice for treatment of most infections caused by rickettsia.p. 14
  • Best means of preventing rickettsial diseases:p. 14
    • Reducing or avoiding contact with the respective vectors or arthropodsp. 14
    • Wearing protective clothingp. 14
    • Good hygienep. 14
    • Frequent examination of skin for ticks in preventing rocky mountain spotted fever, since the ticks should be attached for 45–90 minutes in order to transmit the disease.p. 14
    • Currently no vaccine for rocky mountain spotted feverp. 14
    • Prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended for asymptomatic persons bitten by the tick.p. 14

THE CELL WALL DEFINES MYCOBACTERIA
THE CELL WALL DEFINES MYCOBACTERIA6
  • Genus Mycobacterium: Aerobic, non-spore-forming, non-motile bacilli (slightly curved rods).p. 1
  • Not Gram-positive. Not Gram-negative.p. 1
  • A fundamentally different wall chemistry — acid-fast.p. 1
  • Impermeable to gram staining.p. 1
  • High lipid content dominates.p. 1
  • Long-chain mycolic acids covalently linkedp. 1
(C78–C90),
(C78–C90),4
  • to arabinogalactan and peptidoglycan.p. 1
  • This is acid-fastnessp. 1
  • Carbolfuchsin is driven in with heat/phenol; the waxy wall keeps acid-alcohol from washing it back out.p. 1
  • Extent depends on the integrity and amount of mycolic acid to damage the cell wall.p. 1
GROWTH CHARACTERISTICS: SLOW AND AIR HUNGRY
GROWTH CHARACTERISTICS: SLOW AND AIR HUNGRY15
  • ~18 hoursp. 1
  • Doubling time of tubercle bacilli (vs. 20 mins for E. coli)p. 1
  • 3-8 weeksp. 1
  • Typical culture turnaroundp. 1
  • Explains empiric therapy before confirmationp. 1
  • Obligate aerobep. 1
  • Needs O2p. 1
  • Growth is enhanced by increased CO2 tensionp. 1
  • Infections are usually chronic due to their slow growthp. 1
  • CLINICAL PEARL ⚪p. 1
  • Slow growth → weeks-long cultures → empiric treatment often starts before confirmationp. 1
  • Empiric treatment = Intelligent guessp. 1
  • Not all clinical diagnosis need bacteriologic confirmationp. 1
  • Obligate aerobe + highest PO2 at the lung apex → reactivation TB classically cavitates there.p. 1
  • Resistant to drying, many disinfectants, and standard decontamination — but are killed by heat (pasteurization) and UV light.p. 1
